# What is a unit test?

“If the parts don’t work by themselves, they probably won’t work well together”

(Thomas and Hunt, 2019,
[The pragmatic programmer](https://search.worldcat.org/search?q=bn:9780135957059),
Topic 51).

## Definition of a unit test

::: {.column-page}

::: {.incremental .column}

Unit tests are:

- Test which verify the correctness of a single unit of code.
- Isolated
- Minimal
- Fast

:::

::: {.incremental .column}

Benefits of unit tests:

- Confidence that your code does what you expect.
- Easier to make changes to you code.
- Catch bugs before they are introduced.

:::

:::

# Our first unit test

**Objectives**

- Understand what a unit test looks like.
- Recognise the benefits of parameterized tests.
- Be able to write a unit test which is isolated, minimal and fast.

## Example libraries {.smaller}

Throughout this workshop we will look at two libraries:

::: {.column-page}

::: {.fragment .column}

#### Temperature conversions

You will be writing tests for the
[temperature conversion library provided in the exercises](https://github.com/carpentries-incubator/fortran-unit-testing/tree/main/exercises/writing-your-first-unit-test/challenge).

:::

::: {.fragment .column}

#### Matrix operations

I will provide worked examples from this matrix operations library

```fortran
module matrix_ops
    implicit none
contains
    !> Returns the dot product (a.b) of the two inputted arrays a and b
    integer function dot(a, b)
        !> The two arrays to be dotted together
        integer :: a(:), b(:)

        dot = dot_product(a, b)
    end function dot
end module matrix_ops
```

:::

:::

## Testing the temperature {.smaller}

First, how can we test this library using standard Fortran?

[solution/standard_fortran/test_temp_conversions.f90](https://github.com/carpentries-incubator/fortran-unit-testing/blob/main/exercises/writing-your-first-unit-test/solution/standard_fortran/test_temp_conversions.f90)

What makes this implementation good? What makes it bad?

::: {.fragment .column-page}

::: {.column}

Good:

- The tests are parameterise
- Good failure logs

:::

::: {.column}

Bad:

- Unable to run a single test in isolation.
- Extra maintenance of test runner logic.
- Do not benefit from community development efforts

:::

:::

# Our first pFUnit test

**Objectives**

- Recognise the benefits of pFUnit vs standard Fortran.
- Understand how to write a basic pFUnit test.
- Be able to build and run a pFUnit test using CMake.

## Why are we using pFUnit?

**Supports testing MPI parallelised code**, including parameterising tests by
number of MPI ranks.

::: {.incremental .fragment}

A few other reasons:

- The most feature rich framework.
- The most widely used framework.
- Being maintained.
- Dedicated CMake and Make integrations.

:::

## Standard Fortran to pFUnit

### [Live coding example](https://carpentries-incubator.github.io/fortran-unit-testing/instructor/pfunit-basics.html)

Starting with the standard Fortran test we saw earlier, follow along writing
tests for the temperature conversion library.

## Building with CMake

### [Live code example](https://carpentries-incubator.github.io/fortran-unit-testing/instructor/integrating-with-build-systems.html#integrating-pfunit-with-cmake)

Now that we have written a test using pFUnit, let's build it using CMake. Follow
along to build your newly written pFUnit test of the temperature conversion
library

## Key points

- pFUnit removes the need to write custom test drivers.
- Directives tell the pFUnit pre-processor how to convert `.pf` files into
  `.F90`.
- Assertions can be defined using pre-processor directives such as
  `@assertEqual`.
- pFUnit tests can be built with CMake using `add_pfunit_ctest`.

# Parameterising with pFUnit

**Objectives**

- Recognise the benefits of parameterising with derived-types.
- Understand how to write parameterised pFUnit tests.

## Why bother parameterising?

- Reduce repeated test logic.
- pFUnit handles reporting failed tests.
- Ensures the full test suite runs.

And…

::: {.fragment}

It will be much easier when testing MPI parallelised Fortran.

:::

## Basic to parameterised pFUnit

What problems are there with the test we've just written? What happens in the
case when one test scenario fails?

::: {.fragment}

### [Live coding example](https://carpentries-incubator.github.io/fortran-unit-testing/instructor/parameterising-pfunit-tests.html)

Starting with the pFUnit tests we have just written, follow along parameterising
your tests for the temperature conversion library.

:::

## Key points

- We can handle state setup and teardown using derived-types which extend
  `TestCase`.
- We can parameterise tests using derived-types which extend
  `AbstractTestParameter`.
- These derived-types must be decorated with pre-processor directives.
- Parameterising tests with pFUnit ensures all scenarios run, even if one fails.

# Testing MPI parallelised Fortran

**Objectives**

- Understand what is different when testing parallel vs serial code.

## Writing testable MPI code {.smaller}

Some tips for writing testable MPI code:

::: {.fragment}

### Separate serial code from MPI code

- Procedures which do not call the MPI library can be tested in serial.
- Isolating MPI functionality from serial makes unit testing easier.

:::

::: {.fragment}

### Pass the MPI communicator into each MPI procedure to be tested

- Passing in the MPI communicator gives us full control of the system.
- This allows us to use the communicator provided by pFUnit.

:::

## Testing MPI parallelised matrix operations

### [Live coding example](https://carpentries-incubator.github.io/fortran-unit-testing/instructor/testing-parallel-code.html#syntax-of-writing-mpi-enabled-pfunit-tests)

Let's look at the MPI parallel matrix operations code we'll be testing. Follow
along writing MPI parallel tests for the MPI utilities library.

## Testing more complex MPI procedures

Thus far, we have assumed all ranks should expected the same result during our
tests. However, this is often not the case.

### [Live coding example](https://carpentries-incubator.github.io/fortran-unit-testing/instructor/testing-parallel-code.html#testing-more-complex-procedures)

Let's continue writing tests for the matrix operations library and remember to
follow along.

## Key points

- If a procedure does not call the MPI library, we shouldn't need to test it
  with parallel pfunit.
- It is much easier to test MPI parallel procedures which take in a
  communicator.
- pFUnit will handle the creation of MPI communicators for the requested number
  of ranks.
- We extend special MPI derived types from pFUnit in our MPI tests.
